title: Joseph Merrick, aka "The Elephant Man"
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Joseph Merrick, the man known as "The Elephant Man," born August 5, 1862 in Leicester, England. They cover his childhood illness (later thought to be Proteus syndrome rather than neurofibromatosis), his mother's death, his hard years with his father and stepmother, the Leicester workhouse, his sideshow career under Sam Torr and Tom the Silver King Morgan, the London exhibition across from the London Hospital, Frederick Treves's care, the Belgium tour and robbery, the public fund-raising and royal visit, his death at age 27 in 1890, the disputed suicide claim, his burial and grave marker, and the rumored Michael Jackson bid for his bones. The episode ends with a listener mail about a mysterious woman in black during a lightning strike.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter about Thunderdome and Tina Turner, then introduce Joseph Merrick, the Elephant Man, and explain the decision to call him by his real name.

segments.title: Film and stage portrayals
segments.summary: The hosts discuss stage and film versions of the Elephant Man, including actors who played Merrick such as David Bowie, Billy Crudup, Bradley Cooper and Mark Hamill, and the late-1970s wave of projects: the 1979 stage play, David Lynch's 1980 film, and a definitive biography.

segments.title: Birth and early onset of illness
segments.summary: Merrick was born August 5, 1862 in Leicester, England. Around age five he began developing strange symptoms: swollen lips, a forehead lump, rough skin, a deforming jaw, and a growth beneath his upper lip that resembled an elephant's trunk. Doctors were puzzled.

segments.title: Family, mother's death and hard childhood
segments.summary: Merrick's younger siblings died young. He injured his hip at age five, which became infected and left him lame. His mother, a loving protector and his closest companion, died when he was eleven. His father remarried, and his stepmother and father were abusive. He left school at thirteen and took a cigar factory job.

segments.title: Hawker's license, uncle Charles and the workhouse
segments.summary: Merrick sold goods door to door under a hawker's license until complaints about his appearance led to its revocation. His uncle Charles, a barber, took him in for a time. At seventeen he entered the Union Workhouse, a harsh poorhouse, where he stayed about five years.

segments.title: Maternal impression and medical diagnosis
segments.summary: Merrick believed his condition came from maternal impression, the idea that his mother was knocked over by an elephant while pregnant. Modern experts think he had Proteus syndrome, a rare condition caused by a mosaic mutation, and that neurofibromatosis is less likely. The hosts explain mosaicism and the features of Proteus syndrome.

segments.title: Severity of the condition and sleeping upright
segments.summary: The hosts describe Merrick's severe symptoms: a fin-like right hand, immobile joints, hearing loss in one ear, a skull weighing about twenty pounds, and bony growths in the mouth affecting speech. He slept sitting up with his knees drawn in. They note that Proteus syndrome was first described in 1979 and discuss the timing coincidence.

segments.title: Sideshow career and London exhibition
segments.summary: In 1884 Merrick left the workhouse and began exhibiting himself as the Elephant Man at Sam Torr's Lester Music Hall. He later moved to London, where he was displayed in a storefront on Whitechapel Road, partnering with Tom the Silver King Morgan. He wore a hood and cloak in public and charged admission, reasoning people would stare anyway.

segments.title: Frederick Treves, the exhibit closure and Belgium
segments.summary: Surgeon Frederick Treves examined Merrick across the street from the London Hospital and asked him to be presented to the Pathological Society. Merrick declined further exams, and police shut down the London exhibit. Merrick toured Belgium, where a manager robbed him of his savings.

segments.title: Return to London, public support and royal visit
segments.summary: Merrick returned to England, where he was stranded and robbed. Police reportedly found Treves's business card on him and brought him to the London Hospital. A letter in The Times from hospital chairman Francis Carr Gomme drew donations that let Merrick live out his life. A visit from the Princess of Wales made him fashionable with London society.

segments.title: Death, suicide claim and burial
segments.summary: Merrick died on April 11, 1890 at age 27. The hosts dispute a Stuff You Should Know claim, cited in a How Stuff Works article, that he likely committed suicide. Accounts say he was found dead across his bed after a fall, likely a dislocated neck. His skeleton is still displayed, and his remains were buried in an unmarked grave that Joanne Vigor Mungo Vin later marked.

segments.title: Michael Jackson bones rumor and legacy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rumor that Michael Jackson bid for Merrick's bones, which was reportedly started by Frank Dilio and is not true, though news reports quote London Hospital staff who turned down offers. They close by describing Merrick's dignity and legacy.

segments.title: Listener mail: woman in black and lightning story
segments.summary: Listener Eric King shares a story from Unsolved Mysteries about motorcyclist Robert Davidson, who was struck by lightning and revived by a mysterious woman in a black dress holding a Bible. Eric suggests the hosts look at a possible religious site near his own sighting of a woman in black. Chuck says he is researching ghosts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to email the show with updates on Chuck's ghost research and gives the show's credits.
